title: Battles in the Supreme Court -- Ch. 5: BATTLES OVER THE PEOPLE'S SOVEREIGNTY
keywords: Law must be stable but it cannot stand still
primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- CJP's account of three battles over the people's sovereignty: the print media ad ban in Osmena v. Comelec, the compulsory grant of free air time in Telebap v. Comelec, and repatriation as a mode of reacquiring citizenship in Frivaldo v. Comelec

His dissent against the ad ban, argued with advertising rates and actual computation: media ads are not necessarily expensive, the ban is total rather than limited, and far from leveling the playing field the Court 'has effectively abolished it'

His dissent against compulsory free air time: Section 92 of BP 881 confiscates private property without due process and just compensation and denies broadcast media equal protection, the distinction drawn from print media being 'too insignificant and too flimsy'

His ponencia in Frivaldo, holding that the citizenship qualification for an elective local official must be possessed when he begins to govern -- a liberal reading that gives effect to the popular will over 'complex but little understood legalisms'
sub_topics: The statutory setting: Section 11 (b) of RA 6646, the Electoral Reforms Law of 1987, bars mass media from selling or giving print space or air time for campaign purposes except to the Comelec, complementing Section 92 of BP 881, which requires broadcast stations to give the Comelec free time for equal allocation among candidates

Osmena v. Comelec: presidential candidate Emilio M.R. Osmena and gubernatorial candidate Pablo P. Garcia challenged the ad ban; speaking through Justice Mendoza the Court dismissed the petition 10 to 4 and reiterated National Press Club, holding that no empirical data backed the claim that the ban disadvantaged poor candidates

The majority's reasoning as he reports it: the purpose of Section 11(b) is regulatory, the restriction on speech is incidental and no more than necessary to promote equality of opportunity, and it is limited in time and scope; Justice Puno concurred that the thrust was to equalize political opportunities

CJP's Dissent with figures: citing a major broadsheet's advertising rates, he showed by actual computation that thirty quarter-page ads in major dailies would cost ₱750,000 while mailing 250,000 posters at ₱4.00 each would cost ₱1,000,000 -- ads being cheaper, wider in reach and more persuasive

His answer to the limited-duration defense: candidates need to advertise precisely during the election period, so 'the prohibition is not limited in duration but is, in fact and in truth, total, complete and exhaustive'

The Epilogue of his ad ban dissent: the ban violates the candidates' free speech and the people's right to information; the pro-poor justification is without logic since the ban favors the rich and popular who can afford costlier propaganda; the Comelec freebies are no compensation, as even the poorest candidates have not applied for them

His treatment of stare decisis: more important than consistency and stability are the verity, integrity and correctness of jurisprudence, and as Dean Roscoe Pound said, law must be stable but cannot stand still

His civic case for information: elections are clean not only in the absence of 'guns, goons and gold' but in the presence of 'principles, platforms and programs,' because an intelligent vote presupposes a well-informed voter

Telebap v. Comelec: the Court, again through Justice Mendoza and by 11 to 3, held that free broadcast time was a reasonable condition on franchises, since stations do not own the airwaves and a franchise is a privilege that may be burdened with public service

His dissent there: the State does not own the airwaves but merely allocates and regulates them; broadcasters already pay rental and regulatory fees; and frequencies are worthless without the owners' billion-peso investments, so forced donation of air time is a taking without due process or just compensation

The PPI inconsistency he presses: the Court had held in Philippine Press Institute v. Comelec that print media could not be compelled to donate space, and the print-broadcast distinction is 'too insignificant and too flimsy' to justify the discrimination, since both derive their revenues principally from paid ads

The scale of the taking and the Comelec's own position: over ₱58 million demanded of GMA for the 1998 season alone, with the total for all stations running into several hundred million pesos, even though the Comelec itself recognized the need to pay the stations

His three-point restatement of the Bill of Rights -- no deprivation of property without due process, no taking without just compensation, no denial of equal protection -- and his lament that the Court had been converted 'into the people's unwitting oppressor'

Justice Romero's separate dissent: Section 92 is a flagrant violation of the just compensation mandate; police power cannot justify a compensable taking with substantial loss of earnings, which is an exercise of eminent domain, and the traditional distinctions between the two powers preclude applying both at once

Frivaldo's story: elected governor of Sorsogon by 27,000 votes in 1988 and 57,000 in 1992 but twice disqualified after his 1983 naturalization as an American, he won again in 1995 by 20,000 votes claiming repatriation under PD 725, taking his oath at 2:00 p.m. on June 30, 1995

The legal question and CJP's ponencia: since RA 7160 fixes no date for possessing citizenship, candidates must be citizens when they begin to discharge their terms; the purpose of the qualification is to ensure no alien governs, and Frivaldo was already qualified to govern his native Sorsogon on June 30, 1995 -- a reading supported literally as well, since Section 39 speaks of 'elective officials,' not candidates

Justice Davide's dissent: Section 39 prescribes the qualifications of candidates and their election, and sovereignty 'is an attribute of the Filipino people as one people, one body' that cannot be fragmentized, illustrated by his hypothetical of the people of Batanes rising in rebellion

CJP's answer that the case turns on a choice of philosophy -- literal or liberal, the letter or the spirit, legal syllogism or substantial justice -- and that in applying election laws it is better to err in favor of popular sovereignty

His Epilogue on Frivaldo the man: he sought American citizenship only to escape the dictatorship, returned at the first opportunity, was chosen three times by the people of Sorsogon, took oaths of allegiance repeatedly, and at 81 showed a tenacity that speaks more loudly than any legal technicality

Justice Puno's concurrence: sovereignty is indivisible but need not always be exercised by all the people at once, since the Constitution itself defines which electorates choose which officials; the real issue is the weight of the voters' will given the uncertainty of the law, on which even American courts are divided; and the Batanes rebellion analogy is inapt because rebellion is concededly a crime while voting for Frivaldo was not

stances.claim: The political ad ban is a blatant violation of the candidates' free speech and the people's right to information: media advertising can be the cheapest and most effective campaign medium, so banning it for rich and poor alike does not level the playing field but abolishes it, favoring those who can afford costlier propaganda.
stances.rhetorical_move: answers an empirical claim with arithmetic, pricing thirty quarter-page newspaper ads against the cost of mailing the same number of posters

stances.claim: Compelling broadcast stations to donate air time to the Comelec takes private property without due process or just compensation and denies broadcast media equal protection, since the State does not own the airwaves, stations already pay fees, and frequencies are worthless without the owners' enormous investments.
stances.rhetorical_move: presses the inconsistency with Philippine Press Institute, where print media were held immune from the same compulsion, and dismisses the print-broadcast distinction as flimsy

stances.claim: An elective local official must possess the citizenship qualification when he begins to govern -- at proclamation and at the start of his term -- not on the day of the election, because the purpose of the requirement is only to ensure that no alien governs our people.
stances.rhetorical_move: purposive construction reinforced by a literal reading of 'elective officials' rather than 'candidates' in Section 39

stances.claim: In election cases it is better to err in favor of popular sovereignty than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms; to inflict a thrice-rejected candidate upon the electorate of Sorsogon would be unmitigated judicial tyranny.
stances.rhetorical_move: frames the dispute as a choice of philosophy -- letter against spirit, syllogism against substantial justice -- then closes with a biographical appeal to Frivaldo's tenacity and the voters' repeated choice

stances.claim: Stare decisis should not preserve an erroneous doctrine: more important than consistency and stability are the verity, integrity and correctness of jurisprudence, and the Court has often departed from precedent before.
stances.rhetorical_move: quotes Dean Roscoe Pound that law must be stable but cannot stand still, and cites the Court's own record of reversals

notable_anecdotes: His arithmetic in the ad ban dissent: thirty quarter-page ads in major dailies at ₱750,000 against ₱1,000,000 to mail 250,000 posters at ₱4.00 apiece, with a single day's circulation reaching 250,000 households.

His observation that not even the poorest candidates applied for the Comelec's free space and time, and that seasoned political leaders preferred paying for their own ads -- proof, he wrote, that the free things in life are not always the best.

The ₱58 million of air time demanded of GMA for the 1998 election season alone, with the nationwide total running to several hundred million pesos, even as the Comelec itself conceded the stations should be paid.

The story of Juan G. Frivaldo, twice disqualified yet elected governor of Sorsogon three times -- by 27,000, 57,000 and 20,000 votes -- who took his oath of allegiance as a repatriated Filipino at 2:00 p.m. on June 30, 1995, the very day the term of office began.

Justice Davide's vivid hypothetical of the people of Batanes rising in arms and escaping prosecution under a fragmentized doctrine of popular sovereignty, and Justice Puno's reply that the analogy fails because rebellion is concededly a crime.
Justice Puno's concurrence calling the Frivaldo ponencia 'path-breaking,' 'pro-people' and a decision that 'pierces the myopia of legalism.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' gathered three cases CJP treated as battles over the people's sovereignty. In Osmena v. Comelec the Court, speaking through Justice Mendoza, dismissed by 10 to 4 a challenge to the political ad ban of Section 11 (b) of RA 6646, holding the restriction regulatory, incidental and limited in time and scope, and finding no empirical data that it disadvantaged poor candidates. CJP dissented with figures, showing by actual computation that thirty quarter-page newspaper ads cost less than mailing an equivalent number of posters, and argued that since candidates need to advertise precisely during the election period the ban is total rather than limited; far from leveling the playing field, he wrote, the Court had abolished it, favoring the rich and popular who can afford costlier propaganda. He rejected stare decisis as a reason to preserve error, citing Roscoe Pound, and urged that clean elections require not only the absence of guns, goons and gold but the presence of principles, platforms and programs. In the companion case, Telebap v. Comelec, the Court upheld by 11 to 3 the compulsory grant of free broadcast time as a condition of a franchise; he dissented that the State does not own the airwaves, that stations already pay fees and have invested billions, and that the distinction from Philippine Press Institute, which shielded print media from the same compulsion, was too flimsy to justify the taking. Justice Romero dissented separately on eminent domain and police power. Finally, in his own ponencia in Frivaldo v. Comelec he held that citizenship must be possessed when an elective official begins to govern, so the thrice-elected Sorsogon governor, repatriated on the very day his term began, was qualified. Justice Davide dissented on fragmentized sovereignty; Justice Puno concurred.
